title: When {recipient} asks again
notes: v2: a full lesson, about 9 minutes and 24 screens. Teaching screens alternate with checks every 2–3 screens, the way good mobile courses work: content, then a quick quiz, a true/false, or the phrase builder.
Placeholders as in quiz.json. Lessons always use singular labels: if Q1 is 'both', use 'your parent' / 'your parent's' / 'them'.

Screen types: intro, setup (sets the variant), scenario (first instinct, no wrong answer), content (title, body or bodyByVariant, optional items, steps, dodont, examples, example note, keyIdea, tip, image), quiz (options [text, correct, feedback]; correct one turns green, a wrong pick turns warm, feedback always kind), builder (one pick per group, then the assembled reply), reset (stores the reset for the plan), practice, plan, wrap.
Every screen has Back (top-left arrow and a Back button) and Continue. Continue unlocks after an answer on scenario, quiz, builder and reset screens. Answers are kept when going back.
'sec' is the estimated time per screen; the total drives the 'about 9 minutes' label.
Variants (set on the setup screen) change examples and tasks only. The next lesson never depends on the variant.

v3 (our copy): nine content patches applied to the owner's v2 file, listed in context/frontend/m1_l1-patches-for-owner.md. Subjects are {recipient}, never {pronoun}, wherever a verb would need to agree with 'they'; no gendered or family-specific words.

screens.title: When {recipient} asks again
screens.body: The same question, five times before dinner. It’s one of the most common changes families notice, and one of the most tiring. In about 9 minutes you’ll learn why it happens and what to say instead.
bullets: Why the question keeps coming back
What to avoid, even when it’s true
Practice out loud, then make a plan

screens.body: Your answer changes the examples and your task, not the lesson.
options: in_person
In person
phone
On the phone

screens.title: What would you say?

setupByVariant.in_person: It’s 6 pm. {Possessive} appointment is tomorrow. For the fifth time today, {recipient} asks:
setupByVariant.phone: You’re at work. {Recipient} calls for the third time today:
setupByVariant.not_yet: Many families notice this first. It’s 6 pm. The appointment is tomorrow. For the fifth time today, {recipient} asks:

lineByVariant.in_person: When are we going to the doctor?
lineByVariant.phone: When are you coming on Saturday?
lineByVariant.not_yet: When are we going to the doctor?

screens.note: Just your first instinct. There’s no wrong answer yet; we’ll come back to this.

in_person: It’s tomorrow at 2. I wrote it on the calendar for you.
Kind and practical. It answers the fact. Keep it in mind: we’ll see what it misses.
Don’t worry, I’ve got it all handled.
Warm. Hold on to it: we’ll look at what “don’t worry” does.
{Recipient}, I told you already. It’s tomorrow.
Almost everyone says this, especially the fifth time. We’ll see why it usually makes the question come back.
You’re wondering about tomorrow. We have plenty of time, I’ll tell you when. Want to help me with the tea?
Good instinct. By the end of this lesson you’ll know exactly why this works.
phone: Saturday morning, around ten. Write it down so you remember.
Clear and practical. Keep it in mind: we’ll see what it misses.
Warm. Hold on to it: we’ll look at what “don’t worry” does.
{Recipient}, I told you already. Saturday. I’m at work.
Almost everyone says this mid-workday. We’ll see why it usually brings the next call sooner.
You’re wondering when I’ll come. I’ll call you before I leave, so you don’t have to keep track. What are you doing right now?
Good instinct. By the end of this lesson you’ll know exactly why this works.

screens.title: New information doesn’t stick
body: Memory changes make it hard to hold on to something new, like a time or a plan. Older memories often last much longer.
So the answer you gave ten minutes ago may simply be gone. To {object}, the question is new.
screens.keyIdea: It’s not that {recipient} isn’t listening. The answer didn’t stay.

screens.title: The feeling stays, even when the memory fades
body: Here’s the part most people don’t know: even when the memory of a conversation is gone, the feeling it left can stay.
If the last answer felt rushed or annoyed, {recipient} may not remember why, but may still feel uneasy. If it felt calm, that calm can stay too.
screens.keyIdea: How you answer matters as much as what you answer.

screens.title: {Recipient} asks again five minutes after you answered. What’s most likely going on?
options: {Recipient} is testing your patience.
It can feel that way. But the memory of asking has faded, so this really is the first time for {object}.
{Recipient} didn’t hear you the first time.
Possible, but usually not. Even when {pronoun} heard you clearly, the answer may not stay.
The answer faded, but the worry behind the question didn’t.
Exactly. That’s why the worry is what needs an answer.

screens.title: What’s often behind the question
body: The words are about a time or a plan. The need underneath is usually something else:
items: Something is coming up and {pronoun} can’t keep track of it.
Without a clear sense of the day, plans feel shaky.
With nothing to do, the same thought loops.
The question is a way to connect.

screens.title: {Recipient} has been sitting alone all afternoon and keeps asking when dinner is. What might help most?
options: Tell {object} the exact time again, a bit louder.
The time may not stay. The empty afternoon is the real issue here.
Give {object} something to do with you, like setting the table.
Yes. Boredom often drives the loop, and doing something together answers it.
Ignore it until the questions stop.
Understandable when you’re tired, but {pronoun} may feel brushed off, and that feeling lingers.

screens.title: One pattern for the question that keeps coming back
body: Instead of repeating the facts, answer in three short steps:
steps: “We have plenty of time. I’ll tell you when.”
“Want to help me with the tea?”
screens.keyIdea: You’ll use this same pattern in every lesson of this module.

screens.title: Step 1: Notice the feeling
body: Put the feeling into words before anything else. It tells {object} you’re on {possessive} side.
screens.tip: “Don’t worry” sounds kind, but it can tell {object} the feeling is wrong. Naming it works better.

screens.title: Which reply notices the feeling?
options: “Don’t worry, it’s all fine.”
Kind, but it brushes the feeling aside.
“You’re not sure what’s happening tomorrow, are you?”
Yes. You named the feeling, gently.
“The appointment is at 2 pm on Thursday.”
That’s the fact. Useful, but the feeling comes first.

screens.title: Step 2: Reassure
body: Take the job of remembering off {object}. Short, calm and the same each time.
Promise only what you’ll really do, like telling {object} when it’s time.
examples: We have plenty of time. I’ll tell you when.
Takes the job of remembering off {object}
I’ve got it covered. You don’t have to keep track.

screens.title: Step 3: Offer something to do
body: A worried loop is hard to stop with words alone. Busy hands help.
Pick something small and familiar, ideally something {recipient} enjoys.
items: Make it, pour it, sit down
To the garden or the mailbox
screens.keyIdea: You’re not distracting {object} from the truth. You’re helping the worry settle.

screens.title: Build a reply in three steps
screens.body: Pick one part for each step. Then read your reply out loud.
groups: We have plenty of time. I’ll tell you when.
Want to help me with the tea?

screens.title: Phrases that hurt, even when they’re true
body: After the fifth time, these come out on their own. Each one points at the forgetting, so the worry grows instead of settling.
screens.tip: If one slips out, it’s okay. Take a breath and start again with the feeling.

screens.title: Explaining the whole plan in detail helps {object} remember it.
options: True
It feels like it should. But long explanations are hard to hold on to and can add to the worry.
False
Right. Short and the same each time works better than more detail.

screens.title: Make the answer easy to find

in_person: Put the answer where {pronoun} can see it: a note on the fridge or a small whiteboard.
Then you can point to it: “It’s on the board. I’ll tell you when.”
phone: Ask {object} to keep a note by the phone with your next visit: “Saturday. I’ll call before I leave.”
On calls you can say: “Check the note by the phone. I’ll call before I leave.”
not_yet: If it starts, a note or small whiteboard with the answer helps a lot.
Then you can point to it: “It’s on the board. I’ll tell you when.”

screens.tip: In a care home, ask the staff to keep your visit days on a calendar in {possessive} room.
screens.keyIdea: And mention plans closer to the time: less waiting means less worrying.

screens.title: {Recipient} has a dentist visit next Friday. When is a good time to tell {object}?
options: Today, so {recipient} has plenty of notice.
That gives the worry a whole week to grow.
The morning of the visit, with a note on the fridge.
Yes. Close to the time, and easy to see.
Don’t tell {object} at all.
Surprises can be upsetting too. Close to the time works best.

screens.title: Look for a pattern
body: Notice when the questions come. Is it the same time of day? After a nap? When {recipient} is hungry, tired or has nothing to do?
If you spot a pattern, you can get ahead of it: tea at 4, a walk before dinner.
screens.tip: If repeated questions are new or suddenly much worse, mention it at the next doctor visit.

screens.title: The fifth time is the hardest
screens.body: Feeling frustrated is normal. It doesn’t mean you care any less. A small reset before you answer makes a big difference.
screens.question: Pick your reset for next time:
options: One slow breath before I answer
take one slow breath
Say the first words slowly
say the first words slowly
Step away for a minute, if it’s safe
step away for a minute, if it’s safe

screens.title: {Recipient} asks for the fourth time when a visitor is coming. Which reply follows all three steps?
options: “Someone’s coming Sunday. I told you this morning.”
True, but it skips the feeling and points at the forgetting.
“You’re looking forward to the visit. It’s Sunday. Want to set out the good cups?”
Yes: the feeling, a short reassurance, and something to do together.
“Don’t worry, everything’s fine.”
Warm, but it brushes the feeling aside and offers nothing to do.

fallbackScenarios.setup: Ten minutes later, {recipient} asks again, a little more worried:

answers.text: No, nothing's wrong. I already said it's just a checkup.
answers.feedback: True, but "already said" points at the forgetting.

answers.text: You sound worried. I'm right here, and everything's taken care of. Come sit with me?

answers.feedback: It can feel like blame, and {recipient} may not know why either.

fallbackScenarios.line: Why won't you just tell me? You're hiding something.

answers.text: I'm not hiding anything. I've told you five times.
answers.feedback: Defending yourself is natural, but it turns into an argument.

answers.text: It sounds like you feel left out. I'll tell you everything as it happens. Want to look at the calendar together?
answers.feedback: You named the feeling and gave a calm, shared next step.
It answers the question, but not the feeling of being left out.

followUpsDidntHelp.title: Give {object} something to do
